content:
This month at the beginning, Google released the brand-new Pixel 11 series phones. Compared to last year's Pixel 10 series, the phone itself has not changed much, but there are several welcome improvements in terms of user experience. One of them is the addition of a whole new set of camera image processing options, giving you much greater control over the final look of your photos.

On the eve of the iPhone 18 Pro launch, I hope Apple can also introduce a similar feature.

The Pixel 11 has added a new camera feature called Camera Looks. This feature is somewhat similar to the Photographic Styles on the iPhone, both allowing you to adjust how the camera renders an image before you press the shutter. These adjustments are made before the shot is taken, so they are far more than ordinary filters.

Google offers a lot of presets similar to Apple's, and even allows you to fine-tune the details of each style. They have also added several new options that capture recent trends in mobile photography: Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal.

These styles all keep their distance from that heavily edited look typical of smartphone photos, and instead try to recapture the charm of traditional photography. Digi, as the name suggests, recreates the low-dynamic-range, high-contrast, and noise-rich imaging style of those compact pocket cameras from the 2010s.

On the other hand, Minimal takes a completely low-processing route — most of the HDR processing pipeline does not run, so what you see is essentially the image actually captured by the smartphone's sensor. You can see some sample shots over at 9to5Google.

Shooting in ProRAW on the iPhone does allow you to revert photos to a state with less post-processing, but doing so somewhat defeats the purpose of using a phone to take pictures.

Summary

If Apple wants to build the best camera that fits in your pocket, it has to accept that not every user has the same needs. Photographic Styles is a good start, but Apple should go further. Photography is, after all, an art of self-expression; giving users more options to control the degree of processing applied to a photo would be a major leap forward. Apple should learn from Google and add a 'Minimal' style to the iPhone.

What are your thoughts on the current state of iPhone photography? Do you like how Apple has been handling Photographic Styles recently, or do you think there is still room for improvement? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
